title: Roaring Twenties
description: 1920s period of sustained economic prosperity in Western Europe and North America
wiki_lead:
The Roaring Twenties, sometimes stylized as Roaring '20s, refers to the 1920s decade in music and fashion, as it happened in Western society and Western culture. It was a period of economic prosperity with a distinctive cultural edge in the United States and internationally, particularly in major cities such as Berlin, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Chicago, London, Los Angeles, Mexico City, New York City, Paris, and Sydney. In France, the decade was known as the années folles ('crazy years'), emphasizing the era's social, artistic and cultural dynamism. Jazz blossomed, the flapper redefined the modern look for British and American women, and Art Deco peaked.
The social and cultural features known as the Roaring Twenties began in leading metropolitan centers and spread widely in the aftermath of World War I. The spirit of the Roaring Twenties was marked by a general feeling of novelty associated with modernity and a break with tradition, through modern technology such as automobiles, moving pictures, and radio, bringing "modernity" to a large part of the population. In terms of architecture, there was a departure from more historically derived, naturalistic styles such as Beaux-Arts towards more sleek, geometric, mechanistic forms in Art Deco. At the same time, jazz and dancing rose in popularity, in opposition to the mood of World War I. As such, the period often is referred to as the Jazz Age.
The 1920s saw the large-scale development and use of automobiles, telephones, films, radio, and electrical appliances in the lives of millions in the Western world. Aviation soon became a business due to its rapid growth. Nations saw rapid industrial and economic growth, accelerated consumer demand, and introduced significant new trends in lifestyle and culture. The media, funded by the new industry of mass-market advertising driving consumer demand, focused on celebrities, especially sports heroes and movie stars, as cities rooted for their home teams and filled the new palatial cinemas and gigantic sports stadiums. In many countries, women won the right to vote.
Wall Street invested heavily in Germany under the 1924 Dawes Plan, named after banker and later 30th vice president Charles G. Dawes. The money was used indirectly to pay reparations to countries that also had to pay off their war debts to Washington. While by the middle of the decade prosperity was widespread, with the second half of the decade known, especially in Germany, as the "Golden Twenties", the decade was coming fast to an end. The Wall Street crash of 1929 ended the era, as the Great Depression brought years of hardship worldwide.

Economy

The Roaring Twenties was a decade of economic growth and widespread prosperity, driven by recovery from wartime devastation and deferred spending, a boom in construction, and the rapid growth of consumer goods such as automobiles and electricity in North America and Europe and a few other developed countries such as Australia. grok_lead: The Roaring Twenties, encompassing the years 1920 to 1929, referred primarily to a transformative era in the United States marked by rapid economic expansion, cultural exuberance, and social liberalization in the aftermath of World War I, driven by mass production, electrification, and automotive proliferation that boosted real GDP growth to an average annual rate of about 4.1%. This period, also termed the Jazz Age, witnessed the ascent of syncopated jazz music from African American communities in urban centers like New Orleans and Harlem, symbolizing racial and artistic innovation amid persistent segregation and the Great Migration of over 1.5 million Black Southerners northward. Central to the decade's social fabric was the flapper archetypeâyoung women embracing shorter hemlines, bobbed hair, and public smoking or dancing in defiance of prewar proprietyâreflecting broader shifts like the 19th Amendment's ratification in 1920, which enfranchised women, though voting turnout remained low and gender disparities endured. The 18th Amendment's Prohibition (effective 1920) aimed to curb alcohol consumption but instead spawned widespread speakeasies, bootlegging empires under figures like Al Capone, and a surge in organized crime, with homicide rates climbing amid corrupt enforcement. Economic gains, while realâevidenced by industrial output doubling and consumer durables like radios entering millions of homesâwere uneven, favoring urbanites and the affluent, with farm incomes stagnating and wealth concentration rising, as the top 1% captured 24% of income by 1928. Urbanization accelerated, with over half the population city-dwelling by 1930, fueling consumerism via credit and advertising, alongside artistic movements like the Harlem Renaissance and Art Deco architecture, yet nativist backlash manifested in the 1924 Immigration Act's quotas and the revived Ku Klux Klan's peak membership exceeding 4 million. Speculative fervor in stocks and real estate, unbridled by scant regulation, inflated a credit-fueled bubble that burst in the 1929 crash, exposing underlying fragilities like overproduction and malinvestment, though the decade's innovations laid groundwork for modern mass culture.
